  "body": "A rival posing: this may not be an agreement-precision problem but an over-negotiation problem. Where p.rival.0 reads the breakdowns as low-resolution contracts and proposes writing them at higher resolution, I would start from the observation that a shared flat forces friends into dozens of small negotiations a month — who, when, whether it counts — and each one is a fresh chance to argue. Per-instance assignment is itself the conflict generator, and schedule churn multiplies the instances. On this reading, the friend who avoids the conversations is not only telling you the talks are unpleasant; he may have concluded they are pointless, since previous talks produced agreements that decayed. More talk of the same kind will not recruit him.

Three practical consequences follow. First, convert per-task negotiation into standing ownership: divide the shared work into zones (kitchen, bathroom, floors and bins, or whatever fits) with one permanent owner each, balanced by rough minutes rather than perfect fairness, plus a single visible floor-standard per zone agreed once — 'a guest could use this without comment' — instead of renegotiating what 'done' means task by task. Ownership removes most who-and-when negotiation and makes schedule compatibility each owner's private problem. Second, buy out the worst of it: a fortnightly cleaner for the common areas, or any durable cost-shift — a dishwasher, fewer shared meals — aimed specifically at the chores generating the most disputes, split three ways or weighted by income. Resistance to paying is usually symbolic; the flat would be purchasing conflict-reduction, not cleanliness. Third, before redesigning anything for three people, change the one variable you control: for a few weeks, do your own share visibly well, raise nothing mid-dispute, and watch the temperature. This is also diagnostic — if the arguments continue at the same pitch with you fully de-escalated, the fuel lies between the other two or in the arrangement; if it drops, some of it was yours.

I would also treat the avoidance as a fork rather than a symptom: once, one-to-one, ask the absent friend for nothing — 'I'm not asking you to agree to anything; I want to know what living here looks like from your side.' If he talks, you learn which diagnosis you are in. If he won't, the conflict has probably migrated from the chores to the living arrangement itself, and the honest open question becomes whether this configuration of people should keep living together — worth holding in view privately, because it prices the cost of doing nothing. My departure from p.rival.0 is at the level of pose, not of every move: its write-it-down and time-boxed check-in survive inside mine as the floor-standards and a zone-swap review. But I would not expect higher-resolution agreements alone to hold, because the disagreements you describe sound at least partly interest-driven — each of you remembering the favourable version — and documentation does not much restrain motivated compliance.",
  "commitments": "I am advancing one empirical conjecture (recurring flatmate chore conflict is produced more by the number of negotiations than by their vagueness), one alternative reading of the avoidant friend (concluded-pointlessness rather than conversation-cost — a rival to, not a refutation of, p.rival.0's interpretation), and one interpretive caution (disputes over what an agreement meant are often motivated rather than mnemonic; this is my ground for doubting that documentation alone resolves them, though neither account has evidence for its memory claim from what is exposed). Everything else — zones, floor-standards, the buyout, the de-escalation trial, the ask-nothing conversation — is proposed application, conditional on the conjectures surviving this flat's history: if flare-ups clustered around handoffs and per-task assignments, my framing gains support; if they cluster around relitigating clearly-remembered or written promises, p.rival.0's does, and I would then retract the pose while keeping the floor-standard idea, imported back into its write-it-down scheme.

Dependencies: the buyout depends on spare money and on nobody refusing on principle; the cleaner and dishwasher are examples, not requirements — the actual dependence is on any durable cost-shift aimed at the most-argued chores, so taking this up includes auditing which chores generate the disputes first, since a foreseeable misuse is outsourcing the easy chores and leaving the contested ones. Zone ownership depends on surviving the initial minute-balancing negotiation, which can reproduce the original fight once at higher stakes; my only mitigations are time-boxing it, accepting rough equality, and pre-agreeing a swap window after a month.

Proposed tests, with weaknesses stated: the de-escalation trial is meant to separate the user's contribution from the system's, but it is unblinded and confounded — schedules change anyway, a few weeks is short, visible restraint can itself read as score-keeping, and bottling legitimate grievances can manufacture a later blow-up that a 'success' reading would misexplain. The ask-nothing one-to-one is meant to discriminate my pointless-talk conjecture from p.rival.0's costly-talk one, but a guarded friend may give a polite non-answer indistinguishable from either, so a null result should count as no evidence. The ownership scheme's own proposed measure — fewer negotiations after adoption — inherits the problem that 'an argument' has no stable unit across households.

Scope and unresolved problems: everything assumes the three intend to keep cohabiting and that the friend's withdrawal is chore-specific; if it extends wider, none of this applies. I do not resolve whose threshold sets a common-area floor standard when the three differ greatly (the guest-test I gesture at may just entrench the middle standard), whether income-weighting the buyout imports a status asymmetry costing more than the chores did, or how the 'should we still live together' question could be raised aloud without functioning as a threat — I flag it as a consequence to price, not an action I defend. Finally, p.rival.0's commitment field was not supplied to me, so convergence or conflict with its test regime is out of view; my reliance on it is limited to its body as quoted."
}

Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Write the commitment surface in ordinary free prose, using whatever arrangement suits the content. You may distinguish a claim from a proposed application, scope, action or consequence; mention from dependence; a criticism and its grounds from a later use or revision; and an unresolved problem. None of these is required to exist. A proposed test, its relevance and the commitment itself can be criticized. State what you currently propose to take up without treating that as a truth certificate. Reference exposed material in prose where useful.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

# rival

Explore another way of posing or addressing the problem. You see the account's body; its commitment field is not supplied.

## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.rival.0)

BODY
Your description names three problems, but they look like one system failing in three places. First, the recurring pattern where you agree on who does something and later disagree about what the agreement meant. My conjecture: the agreements are being made at low resolution. 'Who' gets settled; 'by when', 'how often', and 'what counts as done' get left to assumption, and memory fills the gaps differently for each of you. Second, the changing schedules. Any allocation that was fair when agreed silently decays as shifts move, and staleness feels like unfairness even when nobody broke a promise. Third, the friend who avoids the conversations. My conjecture: this is information about the cost of the conversations, not about the chores. If those talks reliably ended well, he would keep showing up. His absence also means any scheme you and the other friend design over his head will fail the first time it needs his input.

If those conjectures hold, the thing to fix first is not any particular chore but the way agreements get made and refreshed. Concretely: have one conversation about the process itself, not about a current dispute — name the pattern of 'we agreed, then meant different things' and propose changing the format. From then on, write agreements down: task, person, deadline, and what 'done' looks like. A whiteboard or shared note is enough; this removes the whole class of reinterpretation disputes at almost no cost. Put a short, time-boxed check-in on the calendar — fifteen minutes weekly or fortnightly — so schedule changes have a predictable place to land instead of producing surprise resentments. Agree in advance what happens when a chore gets missed: a swap, a trade, a small contribution to a shared pot, so one lapse is an event rather than a verdict on someone's character. And speak to the avoidant friend separately and at low stakes: ask what makes those conversations feel bad, and offer the time-boxed format as the answer rather than pressing him to rejoin the old format.

I would hold all of this loosely. I cannot see whether the real fight is about mismatched standards of clean, about money, or about the friendship itself, and your own part in how the conversations go is invisible from here. The procedural fix only works if the problem is genuinely procedural, and the tests for that are in the commitments.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
